quick: 6 mg/m2 IV over 10 min, then laser light at 15 min
Avoid; use only if clearly needed (no adequate human data)

summary: Verteporfin (Visudyne) is a light-activated photosensitizer used with photodynamic therapy for predominantly classic subfoveal choroidal neovascularization from age-related macular degeneration, pathologic myopia, or presumed ocular histoplasmosis. The dose is 6 mg/m2 infused IV over 10 minutes; nonthermal laser light (689 nm, 50 J/cm2) is applied 15 minutes after infusion start. Patients must avoid bright light and sunlight for 5 days because of marked skin photosensitivity, and infusion-site extravasation must be protected from light.
indications: Predominantly classic subfoveal choroidal neovascularization due to age-related macular degeneration
Subfoveal choroidal neovascularization due to pathologic myopia
Subfoveal choroidal neovascularization due to presumed ocular histoplasmosis

dosage.d: 6 mg/m2 body surface area, reconstituted to 2 mg/mL and diluted with 5% dextrose to 30 mL total
50 J/cm2 at 600 mW/cm2, wavelength 689 +/- 3 nm, delivered over 83 seconds
dosage.n: Nonthermal red laser to neovascular lesion

dosage.d: Re-evaluate every 3 months; re-treat with same regimen if leakage on fluorescein angiography
dosage.n: Do not retreat if severe vision loss (>=4 lines) until vision recovers

admin: Reconstitute each 15 mg vial with 7 mL Sterile Water for Injection to give 7.5 mL of 2 mg/mL solution
Dilute the calculated dose with 5% Dextrose for Injection to a total volume of 30 mL; protect from light and use within 4 hours
Infuse intravenously over 10 minutes at a rate of 3 mL/minute using a syringe pump and in-line filter
Begin laser light delivery exactly 15 minutes after the start of the infusion
Avoid extravasation; if it occurs, stop the infusion and protect the area from light until swelling and discoloration resolve
moa: Verteporfin is a light-activated benzoporphyrin derivative. After IV administration it accumulates in the neovascular endothelium of choroidal vessels. Activation by nonthermal red light (689 nm) in the presence of oxygen generates highly reactive, short-lived singlet oxygen and reactive oxygen radicals that damage vascular endothelium, leading to local vessel occlusion and thrombosis of the abnormal choroidal neovascular membrane while relatively sparing the overlying retina.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to verteporfin or any component of the preparation
relative: Recent severe vision loss following prior treatment

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Verteporfin was teratogenic/embryotoxic in animals at high doses. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Verteporfin and its diacid metabolite have been detected in human milk. Avoid breastfeeding or interrupt nursing for at least 48 hours after administration to minimize infant exposure.
renal: Pharmacokinetics in renal impairment have not been specifically studied; verteporfin is eliminated predominantly by the fecal route with less than 0.01% recovered in urine, so renal impairment is unlikely to alter clearance substantially.
hepatic: Verteporfin is metabolized by liver and plasma esterases. In mild to moderate hepatic impairment the half-life is increased by approximately 20%; use with caution. It has not been studied in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Other photosensitizing agents (tetracyclines, sulfonamides, phenothiazines, sulfonylureas, thiazides, griseofulvin) - additive photosensitivity reactions
moderate: Calcium channel blockers, polymyxin B, radiation therapy - may enhance verteporfin uptake by endothelium
Compounds that quench reactive oxygen (dimethyl sulfoxide, beta-carotene, ethanol, formate, mannitol) - may decrease photodynamic activity
minor: Anticoagulants/vasoconstrictors - theoretical reduction of vascular occlusion efficacy
interactions.alcohol: No specific clinical interaction documented; antioxidant compounds may theoretically reduce efficacy.
interactions.diagnostics: No clinically significant laboratory test interference reported.

common: Injection site reactions (pain, edema, inflammation, extravasation)
Visual disturbances (blurred vision, flashes, decreased acuity, visual field defects)
serious: Severe vision decrease (>=4 lines) within 7 days
rare: Injection site necrosis (with extravasation and light exposure)

monitoring: Best-corrected visual acuity before and after treatment
Fluorescein angiography every 3 months to assess for recurrent leakage
Infusion site for extravasation during and after infusion
Signs of photosensitivity or hypersensitivity reactions
Cardiac and back/chest symptoms during infusion
counsel: Avoid exposure of skin and eyes to direct sunlight or bright indoor light for 5 days after treatment
If you must go outside in daylight during this period, wear protective clothing and dark sunglasses; ordinary sunscreen does not protect against photosensitivity
Exposure to ambient indoor light is helpful and quickens clearance of the drug from the skin
Report immediately any severe decrease in vision, eye pain, or injection-site swelling
Bring dark sunglasses and protective clothing to each appointment
pk: Endothelial uptake within minutes; light applied 15 min after infusion start
Peak plasma at end of 10-minute infusion
Skin photosensitivity persists up to 5 days
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light
pearls: Strict 5-day light precaution is the key safety counseling point - photosensitivity, not phototoxicity from sunscreen-protectable UV
Light must be delivered exactly 15 minutes after the start of infusion for proper activation
Protect any extravasation site from light to prevent skin necrosis
Eliminated mainly in feces (<0.01% renal); renal dosing rarely an issue
Contraindicated in porphyria - a porphyrin-related photosensitizer
missed: Not applicable. Verteporfin is administered as a single in-clinic photodynamic therapy session; there is no patient self-administered or scheduled home dose to miss. Retreatment is decided by the ophthalmologist based on angiographic findings.
overdose: Overdose of drug or light may cause non-perfusion of normal retinal vessels with possible severe vision loss. Drug overdose prolongs the period of skin photosensitivity, so the patient must extend light-avoidance precautions proportionally. Treatment is supportive; there is no specific antidote.
